nameStory: This spider gets its charming name from its incredibly unique web architecture that looks just like miniature tableware! The spider builds a dome-shaped 'bowl' suspended above a flat horizontal 'doily' web, creating what looks like an elegant place setting fit for a fairy tea party.
description: The bowl-and-doily spider is a tiny architect, measuring only about 4mm long (roughly the size of a pencil eraser). This small brown spider creates one of the most distinctive web systems you'll find in New England - a complex two-story structure that's instantly recognizable once you know what to look for. Despite their small size, these spiders are master engineers, building webs that are both beautiful and highly functional for catching small flying insects.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for the unmistakable two-part web system: a dome-shaped 'bowl' hanging above a flat 'doily' sheet. The structure feels delicate and non-sticky when gently touched with a grass blade.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny spider about 4mm long - roughly the size of a small ant or the width of a pencil eraser. You'll need to look closely to see details.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Hangs upside down from the underside of the bowl web, waiting to bite through the webbing when prey falls into the dome above.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Small, compact spider with a brownish coloration. The body appears rounded and sturdy despite its diminutive size.

idTips.label: Habitat Location
idTips.description: Webs are built in weedy fields and shrubs, often at knee to waist height where you can easily spot the distinctive double-decker structure.

habitat: Bowl-and-doily spiders favor weedy fields, meadow edges, and shrubby areas throughout New England. You'll find their distinctive webs built in low vegetation, typically in areas with dense grasses and wildflowers where small flying insects are abundant. They prefer sunny to partially shaded locations with some protection from strong winds.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin building their characteristic webs as temperatures warm. Look for the distinctive bowl-and-doily structures appearing in weedy areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak web-building season with the most visible and well-developed web structures. Spiders are actively hunting from their dome webs.
seasonality.fall: Late summer into fall is mating season - you might find both male and female spiders sharing the same web system, a rare occurrence in the spider world.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically don't survive freezing temperatures. The species overwinters as eggs or juveniles in protected locations.

funFact: Bowl-and-doily spiders are one of the few spider species where couples actually live together peacefully - males and females can cohabitate in the same web for weeks during mating season, sharing meals and space like tiny roommates!
confusionNotes: The bowl-and-doily web is so distinctive that it's rarely confused with other spider webs. However, damaged or incomplete webs might look like regular sheet webs - always look for the dome structure above a flat sheet, even if partially destroyed.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sheet web' spiders (family Linyphiidae), the bowl-and-doily spider creates a much more complex structure than a simple sheet. This family includes many of our smallest spiders, but few create webs as architecturally impressive as this species.
compareHints: As the only Frontinella species in New England, bowl-and-doily spiders are unique in their genus here. Compared to other sheet web spiders in the Linyphiidae family, they're easily distinguished by their complex two-tier web system - most other family members build simple horizontal sheet webs without the distinctive dome structure above.
